## Summary

We asked whether bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass can identify an adult penguin from the Palmer Archipelago as Adelie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo. Multinomial logistic regression, fit only on a training set of 257 birds, classified all 85 held-out test birds correctly, so both accuracy and macro-F1 were 1.00. Gentoo penguins are heavier, with longer flippers and shallower bills. Chinstrap penguins have longer bills than Adelie penguins of about the same weight. The main limitation is that these three species are unusually easy to separate with these measurements: five-fold cross-validation on the training set had a mean macro-F1 of 0.986 rather than 1, and the data come from one Antarctic archipelago over three breeding seasons.

## Introduction

Three penguin species in the genus *Pygoscelis* nest around Palmer Station, Antarctica: the Adelie penguin, the Chinstrap penguin, and the Gentoo penguin. Field teams identify them by plumage and by the shape of the head, but museum specimens, photographs, and incomplete records sometimes preserve only a few size measurements. It is worth asking how far those measurements go. If they already separate the species, a simple statistical model is a useful check on data quality and a baseline for later ecological work. If they do not, observers need information the size measurements do not contain.

Gorman, Williams, and Fraser (2014) measured foraging adults near Palmer Station from 2007 to 2009 as part of the Palmer Station Long Term Ecological Research program. Horst, Hill, and Gorman (2020) published a curated table of those measurements. We use that curated table. It is released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0), which allows the file to be stored in a public repository and reused. Each row is one adult penguin. The columns we use are species, bill length in millimetres, bill depth in millimetres, flipper length in millimetres, and body mass in grams. The file also records island, sex, and year. The table has 344 rows: 152 Adelie, 124 Gentoo, and 68 Chinstrap penguins.

The question is predictive. Can bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass classify a penguin into its species? The target is species. The question can be answered with this table because every row has a species label assigned by the original field study, together with the four measurements for all but two birds.

We do not use island as a predictor. Chinstrap penguins in this table were observed only on Dream Island, and Gentoo penguins only on Biscoe Island, so the island name nearly repeats the species label for two of the three classes. Adelie penguins occur on all three islands. A model that saw the island would look more accurate without having learned the body measurements. We also leave out sex and year. Sex is missing for 11 birds, and year identifies the season of sampling rather than the bird's body.

```{python}
# Each row is one adult penguin.
# Target variable: species (Adelie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo). This is what we predict.
# Features: bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g.
# Unused columns: island (almost repeats species), sex (missing for 11 birds), year (sampling season, not body size).
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, f1_score
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.size": 12,
    "axes.labelsize": 12,
    "legend.fontsize": 11,
    "figure.dpi": 120,
})

ROOT = Path.cwd()
if not (ROOT / "pyproject.toml").exists() and (ROOT.parent / "pyproject.toml").exists():
    ROOT = ROOT.parent

# Same curated table as palmerpenguins::penguins in R. Licence: CC0.
# Download from the original URL and save the untouched file in data/raw/.
RAW_URL = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/"
    "palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv"
)
# Predictors used by the classifier. Units are millimetres and grams.
FEATURES = [
    "bill_length_mm",      # bill length (mm)
    "bill_depth_mm",       # bill depth (mm)
    "flipper_length_mm",   # flipper length (mm)
    "body_mass_g",         # body mass (g)
]
TARGET = "species"  # response: Adelie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo
# Fixed seed so the train/test split is the same every time the report is rendered.
RANDOM_STATE = 522
SPECIES_ORDER = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]
SPECIES_COLOURS = {
    "Adelie": "#E69F00",
    "Chinstrap": "#CC79A7",
    "Gentoo": "#009E73",
}

raw_path = ROOT / "data" / "raw" / "penguins.csv"
processed_dir = ROOT / "data" / "processed"
raw_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Save the downloaded file first. Later steps read this local copy and do not edit it.
pd.read_csv(RAW_URL).to_csv(raw_path, index=False)
penguins = pd.read_csv(raw_path)
penguins.shape
```

## Methods

The response has three classes, and the predictors are numeric measurements on incompatible units: millimetres and grams. Multinomial logistic regression is a direct model for that situation. It estimates the probability of each species from a linear function of the predictors, then classifies the bird as the species with the highest probability (James, Witten, Hastie, and Tibshirani 2021). We use the implementation in scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011). Before fitting, each measurement is standardized to mean zero and standard deviation one, using the training birds only, so that body mass does not dominate the penalty term merely because it is recorded in grams.

The model has one chosen setting, the inverse penalty strength, usually called C. A larger C means a weaker penalty. We compared C values of 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, and 100. The comparison used five-fold stratified cross-validation inside the training set and selected the value with the highest mean macro-F1. Macro-F1 is the F1 score computed separately for each species and then averaged, so the smallest class, Chinstrap, counts as much as the largest class, Adelie. Accuracy alone would mostly reflect the larger Adelie and Gentoo groups. We report accuracy as well, because it answers the plain question of how often the species label is right.

The test set was created before any of these choices were inspected. We held out 25 percent of the 344 rows, stratified by species, with random seed 522. Missingness was inspected on the training rows only.

```{python}
# Split before any exploratory plot, row dropping, or model choice.
# stratify keeps the species mix in the training and test sets close to the full table.
# The target used for stratifying is species, not a feature.
train_df, test_df = train_test_split(
    penguins,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=RANDOM_STATE,
    stratify=penguins[TARGET],
)

missing_labels = [
    "Species",
    "Island",
    "Bill length (mm)",
    "Bill depth (mm)",
    "Flipper length (mm)",
    "Body mass (g)",
    "Sex",
    "Year",
]
# Count missing values on the training rows only. The test set does not decide how we clean.
missing = train_df.isna().sum().rename("Missing training rows").to_frame()
missing.index = missing_labels
missing
```

One training bird is missing all four measurements. That is too little information to support an imputation model, and a bird with no measurements cannot be classified from those measurements. We therefore drop any row with a missing measurement. The same rule is applied to the test set. Sex is also missing for some training birds, but sex is not a predictor, so those rows stay. The cleaned tables are written to `data/processed/`.

```{python}
# Drop a row if any feature is missing. Species itself has no missing values.
# The rule is chosen from the training set and then applied unchanged to the test set.
# Cleaned tables go to data/processed/. data/raw/ stays as downloaded.
train_fit = train_df.dropna(subset=FEATURES).copy()
test_fit = test_df.dropna(subset=FEATURES).copy()
train_fit.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_train.csv", index=False)
test_fit.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_test.csv", index=False)

print(f"Training birds before dropping incomplete rows: {len(train_df)}")
print(f"Test birds before dropping incomplete rows: {len(test_df)}")
print(f"Training birds used: {len(train_fit)}")
print(f"Test birds used: {len(test_fit)}")
```

Exploratory summaries and figures below use the cleaned training set only. The test set is not plotted and is not used to choose C.

```{python}
# Training set only. Counts are of the target, species.
# Means are of the four features: bill length, bill depth, flipper length, and body mass.
counts = train_fit[TARGET].value_counts().reindex(SPECIES_ORDER)
means = (
    train_fit.groupby(TARGET, observed=True)[FEATURES]
    .mean()
    .reindex(SPECIES_ORDER)
)
training_summary = means.round(1)
training_summary.insert(0, "Birds", counts.astype(int))
training_summary = training_summary.reset_index()
training_summary.columns = [
    "Species",
    "Birds",
    "Bill length (mm)",
    "Bill depth (mm)",
    "Flipper length (mm)",
    "Body mass (g)",
]
training_summary = training_summary.set_index("Species")
training_summary
```

**Table 1.** Number of training birds of each species, and the mean of each body measurement.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.2
# Training-set count of the target variable. Chinstrap is the smallest class.
figure, axis = plt.subplots()
axis.bar(
    counts.index,
    counts.values,
    color=[SPECIES_COLOURS[species] for species in counts.index],
)
axis.set_xlabel("Species")
axis.set_ylabel("Number of penguins")
axis.set_ylim(0, counts.max() * 1.2)
figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Figure 1.** Number of training birds of each species. Adelie is the largest class and Chinstrap is the smallest.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
# Training set only. Two features: bill length (mm) and bill depth (mm). Colour is the target, species.
figure, axis = plt.subplots()
for species, group in train_fit.groupby(TARGET, observed=True):
    axis.scatter(
        group["bill_length_mm"],
        group["bill_depth_mm"],
        label=species,
        c=SPECIES_COLOURS[species],
        alpha=0.75,
        s=36,
        edgecolors="none",
    )
axis.set_xlabel("Bill length (mm)")
axis.set_ylabel("Bill depth (mm)")
axis.legend(title="Species")
figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Figure 2.** Bill length and bill depth in the training set. Gentoo penguins have shallower bills. Chinstrap penguins have longer bills than Adelie penguins.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
# Training set only. Two features: flipper length (mm) and body mass (g). Colour is the target, species.
figure, axis = plt.subplots()
for species, group in train_fit.groupby(TARGET, observed=True):
    axis.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        c=SPECIES_COLOURS[species],
        alpha=0.75,
        s=36,
        edgecolors="none",
    )
axis.set_xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
axis.set_ylabel("Body mass (g)")
axis.legend(title="Species")
figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Figure 3.** Flipper length and body mass in the training set. Gentoo penguins are heavier and have longer flippers. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap on both axes.
